Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Experimental results show our approach can yield efficient alternatives to conventional TCNs that despite being densely connected, still outperform non-dilated networks even with the same number of parameters. We've open-sourced our code and models for the community's benefit. In addition, we've released a companion paper providing a detailed theoretical analysis of our method's properties and capabilities. Our research demonstrates that pruning the weights along the time axis has a natural equivalence to applying dilation factors, thereby enhancing TCN's core architecture. By sharing our code, models, and findings with the community, we hope to be involved in future research and developments stemming from our innovations. In particular, we're interested in exploring the applicability of our approaches to additional deep learning architectures. Additionally, we're seeking collaborations in the areas of generalizing our methods for multi-channel data and leveraging our efficient networks for real-time time-series classification applications. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reversal is feasible because ALBA's decisions on formula expansions are determined by the logic's axioms and the structure of the correspondence theorem, which is in turn governed by the semantic framework and signature. Consequently, we can reverse ALBA's computations for inductive formulas to obtain their first-order correspondents, which can further be translated to inductive ACDI formulas. These correspondents can then be used to derive the original inductive formula using the algebraic language. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas within two logic categories: guarded logic and the extension of BA logic by the Tarski-Tarski property. Notably, our approach has a significant implication: it enables the computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas within these logics using our reversal method and ALBA, which in turn prompts the question of whether ALBA's decisions on formula expansions can be made more efficient.

using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: regional object description and correspondence reasoning. A virtual 3D grid is applied over the projected bounding box of the target object on the image, and regional features are extracted from each grid cell by employing RPN. Each 3D grid point corresponds to a possible object point, thus forming a correspondence map. Sub-region voting is proposed by leveraging 3D bounding box information, enhancing correspondence cues. Moreover, an update strategy is proposed to fuse the correspondence maps resulting from local features and boundary features. An end-to-end trainable framework is proposed, and extensive experiments demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods on three public datasets. Moreover, the proposed approach achieves real-world application by deploying the network on a mobile device for real-time object pose estimation in daily life scenarios. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Notably, MSDCR's code has been made available on the OpenRecon platform.

In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Within this thesis, Springer examines the relationship between the symplectic group and the orthogonal group, establishing a connection between the conjugacy classes of Sp_n(K) and those of the orthogonal group Ao_{2n}(K). He further demonstrates that the number of conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K) increases factorially with the variable n, regardless of the field K. Besides the theoretical implications, this result may have practical value in evaluating characters of the symplectic group. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, can successfully compromise a 0-1 classification based on VFL. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Code is available at https://github.com/yu410/object-detection-fpn. Published in CVPR 2021, our research revitalizes the widespread adoption of FPN in object detection systems. Two practical approaches are outlined in Section 3 of the paper, which is reproduced below. (Figure and table references have been excluded from this reproduction for copyright reasons.) we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Our results also address a discrepancy found in previous studies, where the relationship between outflows and gas usage times appeared to be affected by the type of galaxy. This distinction disappears when analyzing the necessary usage times for different types of galaxies, revealing a single, universal relationship between outflows, gas, and star formation. This relationship has significant implications for models of galaxy evolution, which will need to capture the outflow-driven limit on gas conversion to stars in order to accurately predict how galaxies change over time. Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations reveal important patterns and trends, and highlight the capability of this method for investigating the dynamics of rotating stars. 

As a further development, we have established the equivalence between our Lagrangian formulation and the conventional Eulerian approach, allowing for the comparison of our results with established studies. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications.
